scenes.tts: A nucleus has no membranes inside it, yet it is not a uniform soup. Each chromosome keeps to its own territory, and open, active chromatin sorts apart from closed, quiet chromatin. Membraneless bodies gather machinery for particular jobs. The largest is the nucleolus, which makes ribosomal R N A and assembles ribosomal subunits. So what holds these things together without walls?

scenes.visual: Nucleus cross-section with three painted territories, a nucleolus and small labelled bodies.

scenes.tts: Read the nucleolus from the inside out. The fibrillar centre holds the ribosomal genes. Around it, the dense fibrillar component begins to process the new R N A. The outer granular component is where subunits are assembled before export. In frog oocytes, the middle and outer layers behave as two liquids that coexist without mixing.

scenes.visual: Three nested layers labelled FC, DFC, GC, with a ribosomal subunit leaving the outer layer.

scenes.tts: One proposal is phase separation. Molecules with many weak binding sites demix from their surroundings, as oil separates from vinegar. But a bright spot can arise in other ways. A protein can bind clustered sites, or bridge chromatin so the fibre collapses into a globule. The three differ when you change the amount of protein.

scenes.visual: Three panels: droplet, clustered binding sites, collapsed chromatin globule.

scenes.tts: Phase separation predicts a threshold. Below a saturation concentration, no bodies form. Above it, extra protein goes into the bodies and they grow, while the concentration outside stays at the threshold. With made up data, bodies fill about two percent of the nucleus at two micromolar total, and about fourteen percent at eight, while the outside stays near one micromolar.

scenes.visual: Bar of nuclear volume with dense phase growing; outside concentration line flat at 1 micromolar.

scenes.tts: So the test is simple. Change the amount of protein, and measure inside and outside the bodies. If the outside stays flat, that fits phase separation. If it rises in proportion, with a constant fraction left outside, that fits binding sites better.

scenes.visual: Two small plots of nucleoplasm concentration against total, one flat, one rising.

scenes.tts: Round shapes, fusion, fluorescence recovery and hexanediol cannot tell these models apart. A protein that fails the test may still phase separate, as one part of a mixture. A protein that passes has not been shown to need its body. Keep the order: what is there, what it does, how it forms, and whether its form matters for its job.
